# How a lesson is shaped and pitched: the rest of preferences.md (streamline topic 7, second list)

Step 1 of the streamline method in `streamline-plan.md`, for one list: every
rule in your preferences file that no other topic owns, and every copy of those
rules in the other instruction files. Nothing in the plugin was changed to make
it.

**Progress.** Built 23 to 24 September 2026 (groups A to W, with X and Y holding overflow copies, and Z added by the check). Checked independently on 24 September (`streamline-tools/preferences-rest-inventory-check.md`), and the check folded in the same day: 649 places it found were verified and added, the first list's rows it faulted were corrected, and the decisions were reworked into a short settled list and the real pulls. The first list is kept as `streamline-tools/scratch/pf_ledger_before_check.md`.

**Snapshot.** The plugin's working tree on the night of 23 September 2026:
lesson-v4 4.2.287 (commit `79426973`) with the success-criteria change
(4.2.288) sitting uncommitted on top. Quotes are taken from that working tree,
not from a commit, and line numbers are the line in the working tree where the
quote starts. Other agents were checking and listing beside this one, and none
changed the plugin, except that the success-criteria repairs (4.2.288) were
made at 03:42 on 24 September while this list was being merged; two quotes
that those repairs changed (O10, T18) were taken again from the new text. The
words are what `streamline-tools/check-ledger-quotes.py` checks, and every
«quoted» passage is the file's own words.

**What counts as this list.** Every section of your preferences file that no
other topic owns: the file's own introduction and contents list; Written Voice
(the core rules, the read-back, the calibration examples, the em dash);
Classroom Norms (the 45 minutes, routines, partner talk, the date and the
objective on the board); What a Lesson Is For (your principle, and the three
questions in order with a `thinking` line per beat, and the tests on them);
Cognitive Load Triage on Scaffolds; How Much Fits in One Lesson; Question
Labelling; A Picture Beside a Word and Visual priority; Reasoning Is Every
Child's Entitlement; Support, Checking and Release (its non-worksheet parts,
and the answer slides); Source and Scenario Integrity; Slide Philosophy (what
the board carries, the takeaway, the presentation rules, the visual-need
boundary, launching a task, the speaker notes); Slide Headings; and Pride
Lessons with the two Teach slide calibrations. Each rule's home in the
preferences file comes first in its group, then every copy of it elsewhere:
the lesson designer, the reviewer, the slide, worksheet, wall and adaptation
designers, the routes, the subject files, the voice guide and the playbook.

**What belongs to a neighbouring topic.** Vocabulary (`VOC-`), the Teach then
Do rhythm (`TD-`), quick checks (`QC-`), assumed knowledge (`AK-`) and success
criteria (`SC-`) are changed and pinned; worksheets (`WS-`) is listed and
waiting. Starters, Sticky Knowledge, The Apply Slide, Practising a Test
Question and Purposeful Endings are the other topic 7 list (`SA-`), built the
same night. The voice guide itself is a topic 8 list (`VG-`), and so are the
reviewer (`RV-`), the routes (`RT-`) and the subject files (`SJ-`); the
playbook is topic 10 (`PB-`). A paragraph inside one of this list's sections
that another topic has already changed or claimed as its own (most often
assumed knowledge's 4.2.287 paragraphs) has a row here marked "shared" with
that ledger's row, so the fold can see it, and is not proposed to move.

## How to read a row

| Column | Meaning |
|---|---|
| ID | `PF-` then a group letter and a number. Groups: A the file's own rules and contents list, B Written Voice: what the words must achieve, C Written Voice: surfaces, registers and printed wording, D Written Voice: the rest of the core rules, E the read-back and the calibration examples, F Classroom Norms, G What a Lesson Is For, H Cognitive Load Triage on Scaffolds and manipulatives, I How Much Fits in One Lesson, J Question Labelling, K A Picture Beside a Word and Visual priority, L Reasoning Is Every Child's Entitlement, M Support, Checking and Release and the answer slides, N Source and Scenario Integrity, O Slide Philosophy: the board carries the route, P a case or a name arrives with its context (shared with assumed knowledge), Q the takeaway said once, R the presentation rules, S the visual-need boundary, T launching a task and the good instance, U the speaker notes, V Slide Headings, W Pride Lessons and the Teach slide calibrations, X What a Lesson Is For continued (from G), Y Slide Philosophy continued (from O, and the presentation rules from R), Z A Picture Beside a Word and Support, Checking and Release continued (from K and M). Three groups also hold a neighbour's overflow under its own heading at the end of their section: E continues D, I continues F, P continues N. |
| What the agent is told | The rule's own words. Several «quotes» in one row are separate sentences of the same rule. |
| When it applies | The condition, and any exception the text gives. |
| Strength | **must** (never, always, only, or refused by code), **default** (normally, usually, prefer), **may** (a permission), **check** (a test the agent runs), **mechanics** (how to record or build it). "Code" means a program refuses or prints it. |
| Code names | Field names, markers, headings, messages or commands a program or test depends on. These cannot change without the code. |
| Where | The file, its section and line. The home row of a rule lists its copies. |
| Kind | rule; your example (how the agents learn your taste); your ruling (your words); duplicate; near-duplicate (with what it adds or lacks); contradiction (a numbered decision below); story (a dated or real incident); pointer; maintainer; stale; code; shared (another topic owns it, named). |
| Proposed home | A proposal only. **PREF-INTRO** the file's introduction and contents; **PREF-WV** Written Voice; **PREF-CN** Classroom Norms; **PREF-WLF** What a Lesson Is For; **PREF-CLT** Cognitive Load Triage on Scaffolds; **PREF-FIT** How Much Fits in One Lesson; **PREF-QL** Question Labelling; **PREF-PIC** A Picture Beside a Word; **PREF-REA** Reasoning Is Every Child's Entitlement; **PREF-SCR** Support, Checking and Release; **PREF-SSI** Source and Scenario Integrity; **PREF-SP** Slide Philosophy; **PREF-SH** Slide Headings; **PREF-PRIDE** Pride Lessons; **LD** the lesson designer's own file, kept for recording and the read instruction; **LD-NOTES** its Speaker Notes Voice; **TV** the voice guide; **TSVP** the slide visual profile; **SD** the slide designer's files; **REV** the reviewer; **ROUTE** its route file; **SUBJ** its subject file; **OT** the output template; **PB** the playbook; **WALL**, **WS**, **ADAPT** the wall, worksheet and adaptation files; **SCP** the slide composition playbook and the other slide references (speech, representations, slide success criteria); **PICS** the picture guide, the image scout and its guides, the decorator and the diagram anchor; **HELP** the worksheet helpers, their catalogue, the helper authoring guide and the helper builder; **TMPL** the template catalogue; **STICK** the stick-in files; **LOG** the build log; **CODE** the program; **STAYS** stays where it is because another topic owns it, or because it is the one place that audience reads. |

## What the list shows, in short

- **1,779 places in 77 files** say something this list owns: **214**
  are the homes in your preferences file, and **1,565** are elsewhere.
  Groups X, Y and Z are not new subjects: X continues What a Lesson Is For, Y
  continues Slide Philosophy (the board, and the presentation rules), and Z
  continues A Picture Beside a Word (K) and Support, Checking and Release (M),
  so that no group runs past 99 rows. Three other groups hold a neighbour's
  overflow at the end of their section, each under its own heading: E
  continues Written Voice (D), I continues Classroom Norms (F), and P continues
  Source and Scenario Integrity (N).
- **The first list was thin, and the independent check added 649 rows.**
  The first list had 1,130 rows. A usage limit stopped its builder partway, and
  seven of its thirteen file groups were then read by a lighter model, which
  found far fewer copies than the rest: the slide composition playbook had 10
  rows and 73 more places, the template catalogue 11 and 83 more, the picture
  guide 7 and 37 more, the history file 12 and 45 more, the worksheet designer 8
  and 37 more, the adaptation designer 4 and 32 more. The check reread those
  files on the full model and wrote out 659 candidate places. Each was then
  verified here against its file: every quote is found word for word by script
  (two needed re-copying), its line is the line the quote starts on, and its
  strength, its condition and its claim about the home row were read against
  the file. 649 are added; 10 are left out as not this list's
  subject (how the plugin talks to you, not what a child or parent reads; they
  are listed under "Mentions judged to belong to another topic"). 40 of
  the added rows keep an "unsure" note where the check or this pass doubted the
  place belongs to this list. The rows it added sit at the end of each group
  under their own heading.
- **Of the 1,565 elsewhere:** 110 are plain repeats; **956 are
  near-repeats** that carry their own condition, example, strength or audience
  (their row says what it adds or lacks, and a fold has to keep it); 100
  are pointers; 234 are rules that live only outside your preferences;
  59 pull against a home or another copy; 34 are out of date; the rest
  are your examples, stories, checks, mechanics and shared rows. The first
  list's "99 plain repeats" was wrong: 52 of them carry or lack something, and
  are now marked near-repeats with what they add or lack.
- **Where they are:** the lesson designer (161), the reviewer (108), the template catalogue (94), the slide composition playbook (83), the voice guide (73), the slide designer (67), the history file (57), the knowledge route (51), the worksheet designer (45), the picture guide (44).
- **The core rules are written many times.** Routine classroom management
  belongs to the teacher (F03): about 73 places. Support stays while it
  enables the thinking (M01): about 93. The three picture priorities and
  decoration (K06 to K08): about 96. Blue asks, black tells, green answers
  (R02 and R05): about 54. Settled wording is never reworded downstream
  (B07): about 28.
- **Much of it is shared.** 594 rows touch another topic: assumed
  knowledge, the subject files, worksheets, success criteria, the rhythm,
  quick checks, vocabulary, starters and the voice guide; and 49 are one
  designer's page mechanics, kept here and marked shared with topic 9 (the
  slide, worksheet, wall and adaptation designers).
- **The decisions.** Of the first list's fourteen decisions, eight are
  settled outright by your own words or by a fold that changes no meaning (1,
  2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 14) and three in part (the order of the notes in 3,
  decoration's relevance in 9, the Teach thinking line in 13); they are listed
  below for you to confirm at a glance, with one more the check found (23).
  What is left is seventeen real pulls, merged into fourteen questions: six
  from the first list (3, 5, 7, 9, 11 and 13, whose two limits are asked
  together) and eight from the check (15 to 22; its other two pulls joined 9
  and 11).
- **Out of date:** about 64 places no longer match your rulings or the
  program (decision 14); each is a correction, not a change of mind.
- **Stories:** the check found three of the first list's "not in the build
  log" stories are in it; 71 of the added rows carry a story, and

- **The code enforces the shape, not most of the judgement.** The check found

## Decisions taken

None of this list's questions has been answered yet. The list has had its
independent check (`streamline-tools/preferences-rest-inventory-check.md`),
and every finding was checked against the files before it went in. The first
list's fourteen decisions were then read again against your "no
overcomplications": the ones below are settled without a question, and the
real pulls follow under "Decisions for Daniel". The numbers are kept from the
first list, and the check's pulls take 15 to 22 (23 is settled), so a row's
"decision N" finds it here or in the next section.

### His answers, 24 September (afternoon), first seven

Put to him as 1 to 7 (this list's decisions 3, 5, 7, 9, 11, 13 and 15). His words:

> 1. I actually don't know why it says nine-year-old. Um, because the plugin is for years one, two, three, four, five, and six, right? So nine-year-old might have been overcomplicating some of the things in the speaker notes. And short sentences uh yeah, for the speaker notes it doesn't have to be short sentences. Um speaker notes are as long as the idea needs, of course, and they're also conversational, so it links them nicely. It's talking to children. It just needs to think how can I talk to children to get them to understand it. Um, there's a good example in week three science on the uh, e-drive. Now, this wasn't made with Codex. Well, it was, but then I worked with Claude a lot to kind of fix things. And I don't know if the speaker notes were part of the start or whether it was part of the fixes, etc. But I taught those speaker notes uh, yesterday and I actually thought the lesson went quite well. So that kind of wording and phrasing and whatever might be something that's good for you to look at. Number two, in maths, yeah, your turn would have its answer slide because that's uh, definite answers, of course. Um, writing, I suppose. It's. hard because in those sort of lessons the answer there could be lots of answers so I wouldn't want the um the plugin to choose one particular answer because then children will think they've kind of failed unless it was shown as an example answer something you could have wrote about etc Number 3. Is this in the speaker notes? I don't want it to give me an exact thing or place to write it. That's for me to choose, right? Number four. I actually disagree with this rule. I think there sh could be drawings on serious material, as long as obviously the drawing isn't something that looks like I'm mocking or or whatnot. But I feel like we could take number four out, you know. Um, number five. Yeah, I want blue means question or like a short task as in like explain why or something like that. And yeah, green is vocabulary or an answer. So we'd have to fix those. Worked examples can be something different. Maybe purple. Number six. A slide on should do exist shouldn't really give them an answer, I don't think. I mean, it should or it could give them a modeled example. And I guess the writing task, yes. Number seven. The you can pass thing, I think we should take out if there's anything in there. Instruction wise saying you can pass, but in terms of actual number seven. I don't get why that couldn't have had a picture.

Read back to him:

- **Decision 3 (his 1).** "A nine-year-old" and "short sentences" go from the notes
  voice. Speaker notes are as long as the idea needs, conversational, talking to
  children: how would I say this so these children understand it. He points to the
  week 3 science lesson on his drive, whose notes he taught on 23 September and
  thought went well, as wording worth studying (for the voice guide topic).
- **Decision 5 (his 2).** A Your Turn with definite answers (maths) keeps its answer
  slide. Open writing, where there are many right answers, gets no answer slide
  that looks like the one answer; an example is only ever shown as one possible
  answer, labelled as such.
- **Decision 7 (his 3).** Yes, it is in the speaker notes. The notes never name where
  children write (which book, which page, whiteboards): that is his to choose.
- **Decision 9 (his 4): turned round.** He disagrees with the serious-material limit:
  drawings may go on serious lessons, as long as nothing looks like it mocks the
  subject. The limit goes from his preferences and the history file's no-drawings
  list. The size half was not answered; asked.
- **Decision 11 (his 5).** Blue means a question or a short task ("explain why");
  green means a taught word or an answer; the exceptions are fixed. A task line in
  blue is therefore right (his 18 September job line is not an exception). Worked
  examples take a different colour, "maybe purple"; purple is already the sticky
  fact's colour, so asked.
- **Decision 13 (his 6).** A talk slide's open question ("Should zoos exist?") is not
  answered on the board, though it may show a modelled example; a writing task whose
  criteria already show a good one skips a second model: yes.
- **Decision 15 (his 7): turned round.** "You can pass" as an instruction comes out of
  the plugin wherever it appears; and he sees no reason the card could not have had
  a picture, so the example that says it has nothing to picture goes. Read back to
  confirm.

His answers to the two left open: "drawing size - yes. worked example purple too".

- **Decision 9, the size half: yes.** A drawing is sized to the space it sits in and
  may be large; "small" goes from his preferences.
- **Decision 11, worked examples: purple**, the same colour as a sticky fact.

## Decisions for Daniel

Fourteen questions, holding seventeen real pulls: two of your own rules that
disagree, a rule that looks wrong, or a fold that would change a meaning. Each
says what the plugin says now, what I think and what I suggest; "yes" takes the
suggestion.

3. **The speaker notes: how long a script's sentences are.**
   - **What it says now.** Your preferences choose sentence length "for the
     idea rather than a mechanical simplicity rule". The lesson designer's notes
     voice asks for "short straightforward sentences" that "a nine-year-old
     follows easily". (U01, U07)
   - **What I think.** "A nine-year-old" fixes the class at Year 4 or 5
     whatever the lesson, and "short" is the mechanical rule your preferences
     turned down.
   - **What I suggest.** The notes voice takes your words: sentences as long as
     the idea needs, in words the children in this class follow. A Year 2
     script and a Year 6 script about the same idea read differently, and
     neither is chopped short for its own sake.
   - **Question:** should "a nine-year-old" and "short sentences" go?

5. **Does each cycle's Your Turn get its own answer slide?**
   - **What it says now.** Your preferences give every Your Turn with
     independent work an answer slide, and keep smaller checks' answers in the
     notes. Your own words in the skill route call a cycle's Your Turn "a quick
     check of can we do this before moving on to the next concept". Three
     copies add a condition your preferences never state: an answer slide
     follows work with a definite answer, so open work gets none. (M08, M51,
     M53, M59, M61)
   - **What I think.** A cycle's Your Turn is written work the class checks, so
     its answers need to be seen; and "a definite answer" is the right limit,
     because open writing has nothing to reveal.
   - **What I suggest.** Every Your Turn with definite answers keeps its answer
     slide, and your preferences gain the definite-answer condition. A rounding
     lesson with three cycles has a short check slide after each cycle's
     questions; a Your Turn where children write their own explanation has
     none.
   - **Question:** yes, or should a cycle's Your Turn keep its answers in the
     notes?

7. **Where "which book, one between two" goes.**
   - **What it says now.** Your routine rule says slides, notes and task briefs
     normally state only the learning action, and the teacher chooses books,
     whiteboards or devices. The Do-beat catalogue says "which book, which
     page, one between two, sitting where" belongs in the teacher's script, and
     the stick-in guide calls a quick marking move "whiteboard work". (F03,
     F31, and the stick-in guide's row)
   - **What I think.** They agree the children's instruction names no place to
     write. "One set of cards between two, at tables" is part of a sort, which
     your rule already allows; "which book" is yours to choose.
   - **What I suggest.** The script carries the handling that is part of the
     task (the cards, the pairs, the tables) and leaves the recording surface
     to you, as your rule says.
   - **Question:** yes?

9. **Decoration on a serious lesson, and how big a drawing may be.**
   - **What it says now.** Your preferences say decoration is left out first on
     serious material, and the history file lists death, persecution,
     enslavement and disaster as lessons with none. The guide the decorator
     reads says the opposite: a subject's sensitivity "never zeroes" the
     drawings, and the decorator is told a judgement about the whole deck never
     does. Separately, your preferences call a drawing "small", where the same
     guide says it "may be as large as the clear space allows". (K07, K08, K22,
     and the guide's and decorator's rows)
   - **What I think.** Your 19 September ruling was about ordinary decks
     looking bare, not sad subjects. A cartoon drawing on a slide about child
     labour reads as flippant. On size, one generous drawing across a card's
     corner does more than three tiny ones, as the guide says.
   - **What I suggest.** The serious-material limit stands and the guide and
     decorator say so; elsewhere a drawing is sized to the space it sits in. A
     Year 6 lesson on evacuees keeps its slides free of drawings; a lesson on
     Victorian toys gets several, some of them large.
   - **Question:** yes to both? (Say which, if only one.)

11. **Blue and green: strict, or with exceptions?**
    - **What it says now.** Blue asks, black tells, and green shows an answer,
      a taught word or the criteria. Against that: on your 18 September launch
      deck you coloured a job line blue with no question in it; the template
      catalogue colours a word inside a statement blue ("The tens column
      changes."), marks a table's deciding word blue, gives a callout box its
      own colours, prints a worked example green even when the lesson is about
      to show it is wrong, and prints a word bank of taught words in black.
      (R02, R05, R16, and the catalogue's rows)
    - **What I think.** Each exception chips at the one signal children learn:
      blue means a question to answer, green means the answer or a word we
      were taught. A wrong example printed green tells a child it is right.
    - **What I suggest.** Keep both strict and correct the catalogue's
      exceptions; treat your blue job line as a one-off. On a rounding slide
      "The tens column changes." stays black with "tens" in bold.
    - **Question:** keep them strict, or should one of these stay (your job
      line, most likely)?

13. **Two limits the copies carry that your preferences lack.**
    - **What it says now.** (a) A slide whose title is a question shows its
      answer, with no exception, where the talk route says a stimulus slide's
      open question is answered by the children, not printed. (b) A launch can
      be skipped when the question alone is enough; the knowledge route also
      skips its good example "when the success criteria already show what a
      good one looks like". (Q01, Q08, T04, T27)
    - **What I think.** Both are right and already in force somewhere; a fold
      that kept only your preferences' words would lose them.
    - **What I suggest.** Your preferences gain both, in the routes' own words.
      A talk slide asking "Should zoos exist?" does not print an answer; a
      writing task whose criteria already show a good paragraph skips a second
      model.
    - **Question:** yes to both?

15. **A picture beside "you can pass".**
    - **What it says now.** Your preferences use "You can pass without giving a
      reason" as a statement with no thing to picture, so it goes on its own
      (after a skip button reached a PSHE wall). The picture guide uses the same
      words to say a raised hand beside them works, "because a child puts a hand
      up". (K04, and the guide's row)
    - **What I think.** Both reject the skip button; they differ on the raised
      hand. The statement's meaning, that you may pass, is not a thing.
    - **What I suggest.** Your preferences' answer stands, and the guide's
      example changes to a word that is a thing. A class agreement card saying
      "You can pass" has no picture.
    - **Question:** yes, or is the raised hand fine?

16. **Where a word bank sits on a page.**
    - **What it says now.** Your rule on the order a slide is read lists "a
      steps list, a word bank" among things that come after the work. Your
      Worksheets section and the sheet designer draw a line: a word bank the
      answer is chosen from, a sentence starter the answer is written into, or
      steps the child works through sit with the question, above the writing
      space; a reminder a child only glances at goes after. (R11, and the sheet
      designer's rows)
    - **What I think.** The Worksheets test is the better one, and it is yours:
      what sends something to the back is what a child could do without.
    - **What I suggest.** The reading-order rule takes that test. "Word bank:
      evaporate, condense, freeze" sits above a fill-the-gap question; "Check
      your units" sits at the side.
    - **Question:** yes?

17. **Labels on stick-in pieces.**
    - **What it says now.** Your preferences say a stick-in piece's numbering
      starts again, "because it is a separate resource with its own answer
      key". The stick-in designer gives each piece the board's own name for that
      moment, so the cut-out, the board and the book all say the same. A
      stick-in piece has no answer key. (J06, J07, and the stick-in rows)
    - **What I think.** The stick-in files are right for a piece glued in beside
      work on the board; your reason fits worksheets, not pieces.
    - **What I suggest.** Worksheets keep their own numbering; a stick-in piece
      carries the board's label. The board's "Your Turn (2)" piece says "(2)" on
      the cut-out.
    - **Question:** yes?

18. **Pictures on printed sort cards.**
    - **What it says now.** Your preferences name a sorting card as a place a
      small picture carries a word's meaning for a child who cannot yet read it,
      and the adaptation designer wants one beside each concrete word on a Below
      card set. The printed card kit prints words only, and a sort that depends
      on pictures stays on the board. (K01, K13, and the stick-in guide's row)
    - **What I think.** This looks like a limit of the kit rather than a rule
      anyone chose.
    - **What I suggest.** The kit learns to print a picture on a card, as its own
      tested repair; until then a Below sort whose words need pictures is done
      from the board. A Year 2 sort of animals into "lives on land" and "lives in
      water" has a picture on every card.
    - **Question:** should printed sort cards carry pictures?

19. **"The words never shrink", and the build that shrinks them.**
    - **What it says now.** Your preferences say that when a Teach slide carries
      too much, "the words never shrink, and they are never clipped to fit": the
      beat takes another slide. The build shrinks text to whatever its box
      holds, down to an 18 point floor, and three guides say so. Two copies
      already read your rule as "never below the floor". (O04, Y27, O76, and the
      build guides' rows)
    - **What I think.** They agree if your words mean "never below a readable
      size". Read literally, your rule forbids what the build does on every
      slide.
    - **What I suggest.** Your rule says it that way: never shrunk below the
      readable size and never clipped; above that the build fits them. A Teach
      line that fits at 26 point is fine; one that would need 16 takes another
      slide.
    - **Question:** yes?

20. **The Roman diary example.**
    - **What it says now.** Your preferences give "know how a Roman lived, then
      write a diary entry as one" as a fair product for a second lesson after a
      split. The history file says "A diary entry as a Roman soldier is not
      history": the child does not know what he ate or where he came from, so
      they write themselves in a costume. (I01, and the history file's row)
    - **What I think.** The history file is right, and the example is only there
      to show an objective that is two lessons.
    - **What I suggest.** Swap it for an example outside history: "know the
      parts of a flowering plant, then write a report on one".
    - **Question:** yes, or would you rather give the example yourself?

21. **"Practise" as a slide title.**
    - **What it says now.** Your preferences list "Practise" with "Do 1" and
      "Teach 3" as slot names a slide title replaces with the move. The slide
      check lets "Practise" through as a child-facing label, beside My Turn and
      Your Turn. (V01, V04, V16)
    - **What I think.** "Practise" names a slot, not the move, so the titles
      read in order stop telling the lesson's story.
    - **What I suggest.** "Practise" stays a slot name to replace, and the slide
      check flags it. "Practise" becomes "Round these to the nearest 100".
    - **Question:** yes?

22. **The working wall's own rules for words and colour.**
    - **What it says now.** The wall files let the designer shorten a child's
      sentences to fit a card "as the first move", cap every item at two lines,
      and swap a taught word for plain words. On the board your rules say words
      are never cut to fit and a taught word is used. The wall also has its own
      colours (blue means a fact, green a method, teal a taught word), where on
      the board blue asks and green answers. (B05, B07, O04, R02, R05, and the
      wall rows)
    - **What I think.** A wall is read differently from a slide, but a child who
      sees green mean "answer" on the board and "method" on the wall meets two
      colour languages in one room, and a cut-down definition can lose its
      meaning. One smaller note: the wall's sheet test says five seconds and its
      card test two; that can wait for the wall's own list.
    - **What I suggest.** The wall keeps children's sentences whole (a bigger or
      second card rather than a clipped one) and uses the board's colour
      meanings. The fractions card keeps "the bottom number stays the same when
      you add" as a full sentence, and its right answer is green.
    - **Question:** should the wall keep sentences whole and use the board's
      colours?

For later lists (not asked now):

- **The voice guide (VG):** the chipped tooth (the assumed-knowledge rule puts
  one sentence of context before the case; the voice guide gives the tooth
  first), and the two read-backs, each lacking some of the other's; the
  reviewer runs only the voice guide's (E01 and its copies).
- **The reviewer (RV):** its triggers for the visual-need boundary and for
  Source and Scenario Integrity miss the invented person and the single invented
  case; it adds "unnecessary support is removed" as a ground your preferences do
  not give. From the check: Slide Headings is never routed to it, though it
  judges the labels that become titles; "read its Lesson Designer parts" of
  Slide Philosophy is undefined (two parts or three, so whether it ever reads
  the notes rules is unclear); the launch trigger cannot fire on a launch that
  exists and is wrong; A Picture Beside a Word's trigger names vocabulary only.
- **The routes (RT):** a Teach board's parts are written five ways across the
  routes, and when a launch may be skipped, five ways.
- **The subject files (SJ):** the lesson designer holds each subject's "doing
  that passes for thinking" for four subjects; a subject file says it has no
  authority over the lesson designer's cross-subject rules, where the lesson
  designer's own order ranks the subject file above them.
- **The designers (topic 9):** the slide builder's overflow advice; the "main
  task in the body" rule said about ten times with no home in your preferences;
  the wall's own list of card types decoration may sit on; inside the wall
  files, "one item per card" against several multi-part card families, noun
  titles against the canonical verb titles, and fixed card titles that read as
  slot names; two colours for a word bank on paper; stacked number lines named
  A, B, C afresh on every figure while unknowns run on through the deck; a
  quoted person drawn on a slide but optional on paper; the section heading
  ("Fluency", "Reasoning") a sheet may keep.

## B. Written Voice: what the words must achieve

| ID | What the agent is told | When it applies, and its exceptions | Strength | Code names | Where | Kind | Proposed home |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| PF-B01 | «How this teacher actually sounds - the register, sentence rhythm, humour judgement and the per-resource voices (model answers, worked examples, success criteria, practical lessons) - is calibrated in `teacher-voice.md`, built with the teacher from evidence-based testing (August 2026). Read it alongside this section whenever you author child-facing wording or a spoken script: that guide owns how the words sound, this section owns what they must achieve. Where the two seem to pull apart, this section's protections (understanding, protecting the answer, access) win, because a sentence in perfect voice is still wrong when a child cannot use it.» | every author of child-facing wording or a spoken script | must (read); the protections win a pull | heading `Written Voice (House Style)` (routing card); `teacher-voice.md` headings | `references/preferences.md` › Written Voice (House Style) · L37. Copies: B09 to B21 | rule (who owns what, and which wins); shared with the voice guide (topic 8, VG) | PREF-WV |
| PF-B02 | «**Write for understanding, not merely decodability.** A child can be able to read every word and still not understand what the sentence means. Judge pupil-facing language by whether the child can quickly grasp the idea, relationship or action, not by reading age or word difficulty alone.» | every pupil-facing string | must | | `references/preferences.md` › Written Voice › Core rules · L41. Copies: B22 to B25 | rule; shared with assumed knowledge (AK-G22, voice) | PREF-WV |
| PF-B03 | «**Sound like the real teacher, not like generated text.** The register itself - natural, direct, warm, professionally credible, and the "would this sound comfortable with the headteacher watching?" boundary - is calibrated in `teacher-voice.md` → Core voice; write to that. What survives any register: mix short, medium and, when the idea needs it, longer sentences, and do not turn everything into punchy fragments, a list of tiny statements or compressed headline language merely because that looks tidy on a slide. Write with the contractions natural speech uses (`don't`, `it's`, `we're`): full forms everywhere (`do not`, `cannot`, `it is`) are one of the quickest tells of generated text, so keep them for genuine emphasis (`Do not touch the wire.`) or a formal test register that truly calls for them.» | every child-facing string and script; exception: contractions give way for genuine emphasis or a formal test register | must; default (contractions) | | `references/preferences.md` › Written Voice › Core rules · L43. Copies: B26 to B33 | rule; shared with the voice guide, which owns the register itself | PREF-WV |
| PF-B04 | «**Keep one manageable idea in view at a time.** One idea may need several connected sentences. Several distinct ideas do not become easier because they have been compressed into one short paragraph or a row of abstract labels. Prefer concrete actions and relationships, especially when the concept itself is unfamiliar. `People can now reach more of the forest` is easier to enter than `increased access`; `the forest becomes divided` is easier to enter than a compressed phrase such as `habitat split and possible permanent land clearance`. Teach the precise technical term when it matters, but do not make a child unpack unnecessary abstraction before they can reach the learning. Write questions and model answers about the people, objects and actions first; attach the disciplinary term to that understood meaning. A correctly used subject word does not make an otherwise abstract sentence teacher-like. Preserve necessary technical language and formal source quotations; the teacher’s own explanation need not inherit their register.» | every pupil-facing string, questions and model answers | must |  | `references/preferences.md` › Written Voice › Core rules · L45. Copies: B34 to B38. Copies the check found: B66. | rule; shared with vocabulary (VOC-H05; its last sentence is the one the vocabulary check found unquoted) | PREF-WV |
| PF-B05 | «**Glanceable means low mental clutter, not a sentence-length quota.** A child looking up should quickly know what this moment is about and where to start. Three connected sentences about one idea can be more glanceable than four disconnected fragments. A large paragraph is still a warning sign when its visual mass is off-putting or it asks the child to process several separate ideas before they can act. Shorten or split because understanding improves, not because a rule demanded fewer words.» | every pupil-facing surface | must (not a quota) |  | `references/preferences.md` › Written Voice › Core rules · L47. Copies: B39 to B41. Copies the check found: B77. | rule | PREF-WV |
| PF-B06 | «**A block of connected sentences is judged on density and rhythm, not only on its words.** Density is how much unbroken text a child meets at once: a paragraph break is where a child reading alone or aloud breathes and regroups, so several sentences run together give them nowhere to do either, and the block reads as one mass even when every sentence in it is short and clear. Rhythm is how the sentences move: a run of sentences all the same shape reads as a drone, and the child stops hearing where one idea ends and the next begins. So in any multi-sentence block a child reads - a scenario, a model answer, an explanation, a piece of reasoning, a task - break at the real turns of meaning: where the scene changes or a new person speaks, where one stage of the thinking ends and the next begins, where the action moves from build to test to repair. The child should see the shape of the block before reading the prose.» | any multi-sentence block a child reads | must |  | `references/preferences.md` › Written Voice › Core rules · L49. Copies: B42 to B45. Copies the check found: B60, B62. | rule (density, rhythm, where to break) | PREF-WV |

## C. Written Voice: surfaces, registers and printed wording

| ID | What the agent is told | When it applies, and its exceptions | Strength | Code names | Where | Kind | Proposed home |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| PF-C01 | «**Several things to do are several lines, not one sentence.** When a prompt hands the child more than one item to work through - three things to find out, four features to check, two claims to match - each item goes on its own line as a list under the asking sentence, and the follow-up (`Explain one of your choices.`) stands after the list. A semicolon chain (`the Amazon crosses several countries; the vegetation is dense; people live there`) buries the items inside one long sentence, so the child has to parse the list before they can start it. The line is the unit of work: one item per line, and the child can tick down it.» | a prompt handing the child more than one item | must |  | `references/preferences.md` › Written Voice › Core rules · L51. Copies: C09 to C14. Copies the check found: C57, C61, C84. | rule; shared with worksheets (WS-F05) | PREF-WV |
| PF-C02 | «**Explain rather than merely simplify.** Keep correct subject vocabulary when the lesson teaches or genuinely needs it. Use a clear bridge when a word or idea is unfamiliar: `which means...`, `for example...`, `it's like when...`, a concrete comparison, a picture, or a brief parenthetical explanation may all help. Do not use the same bridge mechanically every time. Once a technical word has been properly taught in the lesson, start using it normally; a vocabulary card alone is a reference, not that teaching, so a word met only on the card still gets its bridge. Necessary precise vocabulary is better than an easier but vaguer substitute.» | an unfamiliar word or idea; limit: once a technical word has been properly taught in the lesson it is used normally, and a word met only on a vocabulary card still gets its bridge | must; default (bridges) |  | `references/preferences.md` › Written Voice › Core rules · L53. Copies: C15 to C17. Copies the check found: C80. | rule; shared with vocabulary (VOC-J01, VOC-G07: "a vocabulary card alone is a reference" is vocabulary's, pinned) and assumed knowledge (AK-B40) | PREF-WV |
| PF-C03 | «**Put challenge in the thinking, not in avoidably difficult wording.** Deep reasoning, justification, comparison and evaluation may still be asked in direct, accessible language. Formal or assessment-style wording is not banned: words such as `identify`, `compare`, `justify`, `evidence` or a test-like question form are legitimate when they are authentic to the learning or useful preparation for the form children really meet. Do not simplify wording merely because an assessment word is formal: when the work is preparing children for a form they will really meet, preserve the language and structure of that form, so the test's register is familiar before the test asks it. Slides may use that language when it fits, and a worksheet may carry a test's exact form when the lesson is genuinely practising that form.» | challenge and formal wording; exception: a form children will really meet keeps its language | must |  | `references/preferences.md` › Written Voice › Core rules · L55. Copies: C18. Copies the check found: C59. | rule; shared with assumed knowledge (AK-G33) and worksheets (WS-F04) | PREF-WV |
| PF-C04 | «**Different surfaces have different registers without becoming different voices.** The slide carries the tighter, curated version of the voice and the speaker script carries the fuller conversational version - not the other way round. | PF-D17 | «**The em dash is not part of this teacher's voice - keep it out of everything a child or parent reads.** Across the whole pipeline, every word that reaches a child or a parent is written in the teacher's own register: slide titles, body text, speech bubbles, success criteria, captions, a stick-in piece's labels, worksheet prose, report comments. | PF-D74 | «Safety wording is not exempt from earning its place. The handling rule above names the one case where a precaution is required; beyond it, a safety sentence competes for lesson space like any other wording, and it earns a place from what these children will actually do because of this lesson - in the room or at home - never from the topic sounding dangerous. Both directions of that judgement are real. A lesson taught entirely from photographs carried `Electricity can cause serious injury or death` as sticky knowledge: wording no child could act on that day, spending a sticky slot the actual learning needed and teaching children to read safety lines as background noise. A shadows lesson that takes children outside earns `never look directly at the sun`, though nobody handles anything and safety is not the objective, because staring at the sun is exactly what the lesson makes tempting. | PF-H15 | «**Some skills transform a whole text from one form into another, and the material the child works from must be the start form, complete and unconverted.** Converting a story passage into a playscript, an active sentence into the passive, a set of notes into a paragraph, direct speech into reported speech: the skill *is* the transformation, and the gap between the two forms is the whole lesson. The child needs the start form in full, including the very features that get transformed, because spotting what to change and changing it is the work being assessed. Scaffolding the *content* is right and often necessary (a Year 4 child converting a Shakespeare scene should be handed the characters' words, not asked to invent Shakespeare), but you scaffold by supplying the start form fully, never by pre-shaping it toward the target. Hand the child a story paragraph with its dialogue written the story way, `"If I touch your hand and it is not worthy, forgive me," said Romeo`, and the conversion is genuinely theirs: they find the speaker, drop the "said" and the speech marks, write `ROMEO:`, and lift the action into a bracketed stage direction. Pre-attribute that same line in a separate box, `Romeo: "If I touch your hand..."`, and the core move is already done for them: "converting" collapses into recopying with a colon, which is the reformat-without-judgement trap (design-reviewer: "a task that only reformats the material it hands over"). The read-back test: look at the source you are about to hand over and ask whether any part of it already sits in the target form. If a child could reach the finished script by copying your source and adding punctuation, the source has leaked the answer, so rewrite it as pure start-form prose with the speech embedded the story way.» | a lesson transforming a text from one form to another | must | | `references/teaching-sequence-skill-based.md` › Teaching Sequence Specification › My Turn · L43 | rule (only here; with PF-H01 and PF-M01): scaffold the content by supplying the start form in full, never by pre-shaping it toward the target, with the Romeo example and a read-back test | STAYS (ROUTE) |

## I. How Much Fits in One Lesson

| ID | What the agent is told | When it applies, and its exceptions | Strength | Code names | Where | Kind | Proposed home |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| PF-I01 | «An LO often describes more than a single lesson's worth of learning — most clearly when it names both *understanding* something and *producing* something substantial from it: "understand the water cycle, then draw and explain it"; "know how a Roman lived, then write a diary entry as one"; "understand the structure of a volcano, then label it and explain an eruption". Building the knowledge and producing the extended artefact may each be a lesson's work. Decide which the LO is *before* designing the sequence, by budgeting honestly: will teaching every new chunk properly — each its own Teach → Do — *and* the substantial production both fit the time, with room for children to breathe? When they won't, that is two lessons, and saying so is the design, not a failure to fit everything in.» | an objective naming understanding and a substantial product | must (decide before designing) |  | `references/preferences.md` › How Much Fits in One Lesson · L274. | PF-I02 | «When it is two lessons, split at the natural seam: teach and consolidate the knowledge today, ending on the lesson's core idea while it is still fresh; make the production the opening of the next lesson, warmed by a quick retrieval of today's learning. Every instruction and named source, unit or response form must still fit; an existing reference ID proves identity, not suitability. | PF-M53 | «Provide answers/models selectively. Starter with definite answers uses answer-slide. Main independent slide work with definite answers uses answer-slide; means Your Turn, Practise, Use Learning, Do the Task, Apply or Reflect when beat contains work children complete independently. Exact-answer Do beats, Our Turn, smaller checks use teacher-only. The exception is a My Turn or Our Turn completed live on a representation, which uses answer-slide so the slide after it shows that representation finished (`modelling-formats.md` → Live-complete helper): the teacher who drew it skips the slide, and one who did not teaches from it. It opens on what was true for many people, one plain sentence before the name (`At harvest time, every pair of hands on a Tudor farm mattered.`, `Not every Tudor apprenticeship went well.`), with a line break between that sentence and the story. It asks its question about the group, with the named person as the example (`Why did Tudor families like Mary's need their children at harvest time?`). And its answer gives the general reason first and then how the story shows it. The name stays; what changes is who the thinking is about. | PF-O63 | «**The harder half: a prompt written by someone who already knows the answer.** Missing context is the visible failure; this one is invisible, because the prompt reads perfectly to whoever wrote it and only breaks for the child meeting it cold. It wears four shapes. A question can name the property the answer turns on before the child has found it: "what shape is the land where the forest has gone?" is a clue to an adult who knows about the fishbone pattern, while a child looking at the same photograph sees size and damage and no shape at all. A second question can lean on the first already being solved, so "the line down the middle of each shape" cannot be read until "each shape" means something. A heading can name a bucket where a question would tell the child what to do: "What this photo shows us" labels a column, "What does this photo show us?" asks for the sentence, and a child who lost the thread of the explanation can still act on the second. And a sentence stem can be built from the mechanics of the task instead of the thing being learned, so "I put ___ first because ___" yields a sentence about ranking where "I think ___ clears the most rainforest because ___" yields a sentence about geography, which is the one worth having in a book. So read every prompt back with the answer covered up and ask whether a child could tell what *kind* of thing is being asked for; phrase as a question anything a child responds to; and build a stem out of the words of the question it answers. The limit is the prompt whose difficulty is the point (a "what do you notice?", an odd one out, a deliberate puzzle), where being briefly stuck is the work. Even there the child has to know what they are being asked *for*; they just should not find it easy.» | every prompt; a deliberate puzzle still says what it asks for | must (check) | | `references/teacher-voice.md` › 6. | PF-Y08 | «`explanation` is the teaching, as the child reads it: the route from the takeaway to the point where the class can use it. The fact is the destination; teaching is the route; the board carries the route (`preferences.md` → Slide Philosophy, `The fact is the destination`). **The shape this teacher teaches in, more often than not, is four parts in this order, and the board should read that way unless the beat has a reason not to.** (1) The takeaway, one sentence, which is the `headline` and usually the first thing on the board (`Lord Shaftesbury campaigned with others to protect children through laws.`). (2) The because or the so: the reason it is true or the thing it changes, said as a reason and not as another fact (`He wasn't a king who could order everyone to obey him, so he had to persuade Parliament to pass laws.`). A fact beside a fact is not this step: `He was a member of Parliament, known then as Lord Ashley.` names him and gives no reason. (3) The example, which is the thing the class looks at while you say it. **Write it on the board unless the board already makes it obvious which thing you mean**, because an example a child cannot find teaches nothing, and a line restating a picture that has already said it spends the board on words the class can see. It is obvious, and the step stays spoken, when the thing is the only thing on the board, or when the picture's own label names it: a diagram labelled `oesophagus` has written the example already, and the key question does the pointing (`Which part connects the mouth to the stomach?`). It is not obvious, and the example is a line, when the picture holds several things and yours is one of them (a mine scene with a child, a cart and a tunnel), when what they should notice is not in the picture at all (a portrait on the board while the example is what the laws actually said), or when the beat has no picture to point at, which is most of maths and any beat built on a rule. **What you write is what they will notice, not only the instruction to go and look.** `Look at her. She isn't being paid to do this.` is the teacher's own calibration and works, because the noticing follows the look. `Follow the tube down from the mouth on the diagram.` stops at the sending, so a teacher reading their own board aloud sounds like someone giving directions and the class arrives at nothing. Three science boards were written that way on 22 September 2026, on a diagram that already carried the labels they sent children to find. ## P. Slide Philosophy: a case or a name arrives with its context, and the structure a task points at (shared with assumed knowledge)

| ID | What the agent is told | When it applies, and its exceptions | Strength | Code names | Where | Kind | Proposed home |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| PF-P01 | «**A case arrives with the context that makes it make sense.** A lesson builds carefully and then drops one in from nowhere: a Year 4 science deck taught enamel, dentine and pulp and then showed a chipped tooth and asked which layer was uncovered, having never said that teeth chip, why they chip, or that this happens to real people. The beat itself was right and the class met it as something abstract, random and sudden. The cost is not confusion about the task, which is answerable either way; it is that the child has nothing to attach it to, so the answer is a guess at a diagram rather than a thought about a tooth. One sentence, before the case, in the words the class hears, is usually the whole repair: teeth chip when we bite something too hard, and when that happens the covering comes off in one spot. The same applies to a scenario, an invented person or a number problem's situation. The test: could a child say why they are being shown this, before they are asked the question about it?» | a case, scenario, invented person or number problem's situation | must | | `references/preferences.md` › Slide Philosophy › Lesson Designer content boundaries · L559. Copies: P04 | shared with assumed knowledge (AK-B04, B05; its decision 4) | STAYS |
| PF-P02 | «**A name, or a thing the class has never met, arrives with its context in the sentence that brings it in.** A named person, place, organisation or event, in any subject, is explained where it first appears on the board, in a clause a child can hold (`Queen Elizabeth I, who ruled England in Tudor times`); so is a thing the lesson meets on the way that the class has never met (an order, a steam engine). For these, the repair is in how the teaching is worded; a vocabulary card alone does not do it. What the lesson exists to teach is taught, and a word the teaching leans on takes the three repairs in `Vocabulary` → `A word the teaching leans on is taught`. Rather than `Elizabeth I said this`, set the scene: `Elizabeth I was the Queen of England at that time. She was worried about ..., so she wrote something called an order. This is it.`, and then show the order. Rather than `one was powered by a steam engine`, `one was powered by a steam engine, which is a ...`. A name or a thing thrown on the board with nothing around it is one more thing a child cannot use, and a board with several is too much to take in. A name an earlier lesson taught gets a short reminder where it first appears today (`Lord Shaftesbury, who we met last week, ...`), never a reteach. The test is the one in `Orientation is not automatically a Teach chunk`: read any slide on its own and see what it is doing and why, or go back one or two slides and see why.» | a named person, place, organisation or event, and a thing the class has never met | must | review page names list (`design-review-packet.py`) | `references/preferences.md` › Slide Philosophy › Lesson Designer content boundaries · L561. Copies: P05 to P08. Copies the check found: P11, P13. | shared with assumed knowledge (its decision 4, written in 4.2.287; AK-C01 for the reminder of an earlier lesson's name; pinned) | STAYS |
| PF-P03 | «**Show the structure a task points at, not only its name.** When a beat asks children to record into or read off a structure — fill a results table, look down a column, sort into a diagram, complete a labelled model — that structure belongs on the board, not only on the child's sheet. Put the empty frame on the slide where the work happens: it gives every child the shape to reproduce, gives the teacher something to point to and model live, and lets a later instruction that refers back to it land for the whole class. "Look down your conductor column — what is the same about all of them?" reads as a reference with its referent missing when no column is on screen; with the two-column table shown, the teacher runs that discussion off the board and the child who built their table differently still has the shared picture to look at. The cost is one visual the engine can already draw (a `table`, a Venn, a labelled diagram); the gain is that the task and its follow-up stop depending on twenty-eight separate sheets all looking the same. This is the same instinct as keeping success criteria visible while children work: the thing the task refers to has to be where they can see it.» | a beat recording into or reading off a structure | must |  | `references/preferences.md` › Slide Philosophy › Lesson Designer content boundaries · L563. Copies: P09. Copies the check found: P14, P15. | shared with assumed knowledge (AK-B27), success criteria (SC-A08) and worksheets (WS-I13) | STAYS |
| PF-P04 | «A slide usually carries a particular thing and a general statement about it, and the order they are written in is not the order they should be read in. A Year 4 science slide showed one chipped tooth and said:» «The class is looking at the tooth, so the first sentence they read should be about the tooth. The teacher's own order:» «This tooth has lost a piece of enamel. > Sometimes, teeth can be chipped or broken if they take a hard knock.» «So when a slide has a thing on it, the sentence about that thing goes first. ## Q. Slide Philosophy: the takeaway, said once, and which sentence it is

| ID | What the agent is told | When it applies, and its exceptions | Strength | Code names | Where | Kind | Proposed home |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| PF-Q01 | «**The slide carries the takeaway, not only the prompt, and the takeaway answers the question the title asked.** When a slide title is a question ("Why does it matter?", "Where did the Mayans live?"), the answer the lesson establishes must appear on the slide somewhere visible: a short key sentence, a labelled outcome, a banner reveal. A title that asks a question with no visible answer leaves the actual learning living in speaker notes; children look up at supporting examples and don't know what they're meant to remember. The teacher's voice elaborates and connects, and the slide carries the sentence.» | a slide whose title is a question | must |  | `references/preferences.md` › Slide Philosophy › Lesson Designer content boundaries · L575. Copies: Q06 to Q09. Copies the check found: Q40. | rule (decision 13) | PREF-SP |
| PF-Q02 | «It carries it once. A Teach slide has a title, a headline, an explanation and a takeaway available to it, and a slide that fills all of them with the same idea has said one sentence four ways: a teeth slide printed `Incisors cut; canines help tear.` as its headline, `Their thin biting edges meet to cut through food` in a card and `Incisors cut food and canines help tear food.` as its star line, and a child reading it met one fact three times and looked at the teeth for none of them. The landed sentence is written once, as the headline or as the sticky fact this slide lands, never both; the explanation is the route to it (what the class already has, the new thing, the look), never the sentence again in other words; the title asks the question or names the move. What the class then has to look at is the thing and the question, which is where the learning was meant to happen, and the teacher's voice does what the pride lessons say it does: fills the rest. The validator refuses a headline, explanation line and takeaway that repeat each other.» | a Teach slide's title, headline, explanation and takeaway | must (code) | `headline`, `explanation`, `takeaway` (`kind` text or sticky); validator: "is the headline, or the sticky fact the takeaway references, never both" | `references/preferences.md` › Slide Philosophy › Lesson Designer content boundaries · L577. Copies: Q10 to Q21. Copies the check found: Q32. | rule with an undated example (the teeth slide saying one fact three times) | PREF-SP |
| PF-Q03 | «The half that is easy to miss is *which* sentence. A true statement about the topic is not the same as an answer to the question on the board, and it satisfies the rule in form while leaving the teaching gap wide open. A slide headed "Why are rainforests in hot places?" whose key sentence says where rainforests grow has stated a fact and never given the reason, so the actual explanation (the sun strikes most directly at the Equator) survives only in the notes, and a teacher whose own subject knowledge is thin cannot teach the slide from what is on it. That is the test worth running: read the title and the key sentence back to back, and check the second answers the first. When it doesn't, the sentence to put on the slide is the because, not another fact about the topic. A title that is a plain label rather than a question ("The Amazon rainforest") asks nothing, so it needs the idea children should carry away rather than an answer.» | the key sentence against the title; a plain-label title needs the idea to carry away | check | | `references/preferences.md` › Slide Philosophy › Lesson Designer content boundaries · L579. Copies: Q22 to Q24 | rule with its example (why rainforests are in hot places) | PREF-SP |
| PF-Q04 | «The other half of *which sentence* is what it adds to the picture already on the slide. Words and figure are read together, so text beside a visual has to carry what the visual cannot: a sentence naming what the diagram's own labels already name spends the board twice and teaches nothing. "A tropical rainforest has four layers: the emergent layer, the canopy layer, the understorey layer and the forest floor", set beside a cross section already labelled with those four names, is a whole text panel spent on a caption while the lesson's actual content (what each layer is *like*, and why) stays in the speaker notes. A restatement of the *pattern* fails the same way even when it sounds like an explanation: "the higher the layer, the more sunlight it gets", beside arrows the child can see thinning as they go down, says only what the picture says. So ask of any text sharing a slide with a figure: what does this say that the rest of the slide has not already said? The cause behind the pattern, the misconception to head off, the takeaway to remember, a definition, a number with its unit: all of those pass, and when the answer is nothing, the fix is to replace that text rather than to shorten it.» | text sharing a slide with a figure | must |  | `references/preferences.md` › Slide Philosophy › Lesson Designer content boundaries · L581. Copies: Q25 to Q28. Copies the check found: Q34, Q36, Q37, Q39. | rule with its example (the four rainforest layers) | PREF-SP |
| PF-Q05 | «The slide's closing line is where this costs most, because it is the largest text and the last thing read: a band along the bottom that recaps the captions two inches above it spends the one line children were always going to keep, while the line worth keeping ("if you want to find animals in a rainforest, look up") stays in the notes. A closing line also has to respect the distinctions the slide has just drawn: "the top two layers are bright, windy and rainy", ending a slide that has just shown the emergent taking the full weather and the canopy sheltering beneath it, undoes in one sentence the difference the slide spent its whole width making. So summarise across parts only where they genuinely behave alike, and where they don't, close on what the parts have taught rather than on an average of them. Where the figure itself can hold the words, prefer that: the drawn helpers increasingly take a short note per part (`rainforest-layers` takes a `notes` map, `label-diagram` its labels and leaders), and a few words sitting on the part they explain outteach any paragraph beside it, which also leaves the slide's one prominent line free for the takeaway. The limit: a meaning that genuinely cannot be drawn still earns its sentence, and then it should be the *largest* text on the slide rather than a caption tucked beside the picture.» | the closing line; a meaning that cannot be drawn keeps its sentence, as the largest text | must; default (words on the figure) | `rainforest-layers` `notes`; `label-diagram` labels | `references/preferences.md` › Slide Philosophy › Lesson Designer content boundaries · L583. ## S. Slide Philosophy: the visual-need boundary (show the class the thing)

| PF-S01 | «**Show the class the thing the slide is talking about.** The question to ask of every slide is `does this name something that exists in the world?` - a church, a carol service, a Bible, a food, a coin, a place, a building, an object, a person doing something. When it does, the class should be able to see it while the teacher explains. That picture is what a child looks at while you talk, what you point at, what they hook their own experience on to, and what they ask an unplanned question about. It earns its place on that alone, and nothing has to be decided from it.» | every slide that names something in the world | must | heading `Lesson Designer visual-need boundary` (routing card; the vocabulary rules cite it) | `references/preferences.md` › Slide Philosophy › Lesson Designer visual-need boundary · L631. Refusing the picture because it proves nothing holds it to a standard the sentence beside it never sits, and the subjects where it bites are the ones whose content is belief, feeling, rule or relationship rather than an observable fact. A Year 4 RE lesson on what Christmas means reached a class with a nativity, a carol service and a Bible all available and none of them requested, on the reasoning that meaning cannot be inferred from the appearance of a celebration. That is backwards: an invented person needs showing more than a real one does, not less, because showing them is the only thing that makes a child treat the words as somebody's rather than as an exercise. The common task is a written prediction: when the beat asks children to predict, the prediction prompt and its sentence stem ("I think ___ because ___") go on the slide, because writing the prediction is something the child *does*, and a task left only in the speaker notes simply won't happen for a teacher who delivers from the board. What stays in the notes is the *framing* — the why-it-matters, the orientation, the teacher's delivery voice. When the beat includes a prediction, also add an investigation brief to the slide: one to two lines that tell children what they will do and what they will have. The teacher's framing colours the task for the room; the investigation brief is the child's prerequisite — a prediction about an undescribed investigation is a guess, not reasoning, so the brief that enables the prediction belongs on the slide alongside the prediction prompt, not in the teacher's script. A Set the Task slide that paraphrases the question in a text block alongside the SC ends up as a wall of black text, and a child looking up is forced into comprehension instead of preparing to act — so keep on the slide the question (on the title), the SC ("your job today") in a panel, the visual hook, the investigation brief (if a prediction follows), and the prediction prompt the child writes from. Everything else is the teacher's voice.» | a Set the Task slide | must | `investigationBrief`, `pupilInstruction` | `references/teaching-sequence-task-centred.md` › Teaching Sequence Specification › Set the Task · L15 | near-duplicate of PF-S08 (framing in the notes, the task on the slide; the prediction and its stem on the slide): adds the investigation brief (one or two lines, the child's prerequisite for a prediction) and the slide's list (the question on the title, the criteria in a panel, the visual hook); restates PF-R08's wall of black text; shared with assumed knowledge (AK-B44) | STAYS (ROUTE) |

## T. Slide Philosophy: launching a task, and the good instance

| ID | What the agent is told | When it applies, and its exceptions | Strength | Code names | Where | Kind | Proposed home |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| PF-T01 | «**Giving a task its instructions is not launching it.** Before a substantial task, children may need to know why they are doing it now, what they are making, what a good one looks like and how the work will run, and only then the instruction. Those are beats on the board, not framing prose: the why is one line that gives the class something to hold while they look at the model, and **when the task is about a particular case, that line is the case and the question, not a recap of the teaching**. A child looking at a strong answer beside a weak one with no question in mind is looking at writing; a child who has just met Sam and his squash is looking for how to answer about Sam. So the case comes first, on a short slide of its own before the model, carrying who it is, what happened and what they are being asked - and the task slide keeps the case as well, because that is the board they write from.» | before a substantial task | must | `strong-and-weak`, `steps` | `references/preferences.md` › Slide Philosophy › Lesson Designer visual-need boundary · L641. Copies: T12 to T20. | PF-T02 | «A recap of what the lesson established (`We've found what our agreement needs: joining in, passing, privacy, questions, help`) is the right line only when the product is the class's own work on what they have just built and there is no case to set; where the strong instance already says the chain, the recap is the same thing said worse and goes; what good looks like is an example beside a non-example with the difference named (`Be respectful` tells you nothing to do; `Listen while someone else is speaking` does); the how is the steps in the order children take them (make one, combine your group's, agree ours).» | the why line, what good looks like, the how | must |  | `references/preferences.md` › Slide Philosophy › Lesson Designer visual-need boundary · L641. Copies: T21. Copies the check found: T53. | rule (when a recap is right; example beside non-example; steps in order) (decision 2) | PREF-SP (the launch) |
| PF-T03 | «**`steps` are stages of work, not the standard said again.** The teacher deleted a whole steps slide from the tooth deck on 18 September 2026 and the lesson lost nothing: `read what happened to Sam` came after two slides showing Sam, `use the four steps on the board, in order` pointed at the criteria panel on the next slide, `write it as sentences, not as a list` was what the two cards above had just shown, and `read it back: does each sentence say what caused the next one?` was the difference line word for word. The test on each step is whether the class would lose anything it cannot already see if that step were deleted. A task whose work is one sustained go, launched with a model and with the criteria visible while children work, usually leaves `steps` empty; stages earn the field when they really happen in an order and the later ones are invisible until the earlier ones are done.» | a launch's `steps` | must | `steps` | `references/preferences.md` › Slide Philosophy › Lesson Designer visual-need boundary · L641. | PF-T07 | «**The same case** gives children a complete good one of exactly what they are about to make, which is what a class most often needs and what the teacher asked for on 18 September 2026: `it gives them an example of actually how to do it, what it looks like ... its not on the board when theyre practising, so its all them`. ## Names the code depends on, and what the code enforces

**Headings a program reads by exact title.** The reviewer's routing card
(`design-review-packet.py`) names `Written Voice (House Style)`, `Classroom
Norms`, `Slide Philosophy`, `Cognitive Load Triage on Scaffolds`, `How Much
Fits in One Lesson`, `Question Labelling`, `A Picture Beside a Word`, `Lesson
Designer visual-need boundary`, `Reasoning Is Every Child's Entitlement`,
`Support, Checking and Release` and `Source and Scenario Integrity`, and reads
`Pride Lessons (Quality Anchor)` and `What a Lesson Is For` every review. The
agents' reading routes name, through `read-reference.py`, `Written Voice (House
Style) > Core rules`, the three Lesson Designer parts of Slide Philosophy and
`Speaker notes hand-off`; the wall and stick-in designers name one paragraph by
its opening words (`Three habits keep any printed c...`, C07). Tests pin several
headings and bold leads by their words (see below).

**Fields and markers.** `unlocks` and `thinking` (each has a length limit;
`thinking` may be empty only where the teacher acts, never on a Teach),
`concepts` (an idea must be met on more than one instance, and not only where
the teacher acts), `lesson.lo` and `lesson.displayedLo` (the display is the
objective word for word or its opening cut; no "LO:"), `lesson.scope`,
`deferredLearning` and `lesson2Direction` (empty for a complete lesson, filled
for a split), each beat's `minutes` (1 to 25; the sum refused over 50, aiming at
45), `durationMinutes` (required by the design check and shown to the reviewer; only the minutes check ignores it, and a design with any untimed beat is never added up), `headline`, `explanation` and `takeaway`

## His answers of 4 October 2026 (after judging 105 slide pairs blind)

Recorded here because they change two colour paragraphs this ledger pins (HOME-COL-PROFILE-03 and -04 in `scripts/tests/colours_ledger_pins.json`).

- On gaps: "I would say that I want a blank line gap between separate ideas in explanations and model answers." Tight single line breaks stay for a poem's lines, a worked calculation and a short run read as one list.
- On colour: "As for color, I guess so. Any card of three or more black sentences gets its key line in orange. Is this going to work for every single thing though?" It does not suit every card, so the rule carries limits: one orange line per slide, chosen by what the line says; none where the lines are equals (a poem, a list, a sequence); none inside a case or quotation the task runs on, which is supplied orange as a whole; never the sticky line, a question or a line with a taught word. The measure is three sentences or about thirty words, because the card he marked on the digestive system deck (`all that black text needs colour`) was two long sentences.
- What this replaces: his 12 September bound `Not on every Teach slide` and the playbook's `Reach for layout first`. The orange line is now the ordinary treatment of a long black card.
- In his slide notes that day he also asked for: the pencil on tasks and the tick on answer slides; no lightning bolt on answer slides; the main task in a card, not the top-right cue; a question said once, not as title and again in the body. Those are built in the slide builder and the playbook (see `evaluations/slide-designer-context-2026-10-04/`).
